extracted.intended_audience: Catholic learners / catechism students (especially children and new faithful)
extracted.subtask_description: Catechetical guidance explaining what prayer is, how and when to pray, proper use of sacramentals (rosary, scapular), and the meaning and observance of the Ten Commandments and the First Commandment. Aimed to teach correct beliefs, practices, and avoidances for living the Catholic faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of prayer
rubrics_metrics.description: Prayer is the lifting up of our minds and hearts to God to adore Him, to thank Him for His benefits, to ask His forgiveness, and to beg of Him all the graces we need whether for soul or body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes both mind and heart: mere recitation is not prayer (parrot or phonograph examples). Prayer depends on the way words are said; mental prayer (silent meditation) is the best form because it requires thought and attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental prayer (meditation) as preferred method
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental prayer—thinking of God, His goodness, our sins, Heaven, Hell, death, and the purpose of life—is the best prayer because it involves attentive thought rather than mere vocal recitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: 1) Remember you are in God's presence. 2) Take a subject (e.g., the Crucifixion). 3) Form a mental picture and imagine yourself there. 4) Examine choices, feel sorrow for sin, form a resolution, thank God. Suggested duration: ~15 minutes or longer. Priests/religious use mental prayer frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocal prayer vs. mental prayer
rubrics_metrics.description: Vocal prayer is the spoken prayers (e.g., Our Father, Hail Mary); it can be said without attention and therefore is inferior to mental prayer unless spoken with true attention and devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not always rely on printed prayers or hurry through them; speak to God in simple words when appropriate. When the Church prescribes prayers (divine office, Our Father, Hail Mary, Creed) prefer them because the Church's petition is joined to yours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer is necessary for salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prayer is necessary to salvation—without prayer no one having the use of reason can be saved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This refers especially to those who never pray at all; occasional neglect through forgetfulness is distinguished from total omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate times and occasions to pray
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular times to pray: Sundays and holy days, every morning and night, and in all dangers, temptations, and afflictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morning prayer asks God's grace for the day; night prayer is thanksgiving and protection. In danger or affliction (illness, death in family, etc.) one should pray specially.

rubrics_metrics.name: How one should pray (five dispositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: One should pray, first, with attention; second, with a sense of helplessness and dependence on God; third, with a great desire for the graces begged; fourth, with trust in God's goodness; fifth, with perseverance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention: prepare and think before praying. Dependence: recognize need of God. Desire & trust: pray simply and humbly as a child. Perseverance: continue even when immediate results are not seen. Prayer should be a conversation—after speaking, listen to conscience/good thoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance and trust in prayer (reasons prayers may be denied)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persist in prayer even if answer seems delayed; God may withhold requests for reasons such as improper disposition, the request not being for our spiritual good, or to teach perseverance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: story of the persistent child; St. Monica's decades of prayer for Augustine. Three reasons prayers might not be granted: improper manner (lack of attention, humility, patience), request not for spiritual good, or God withholding to build virtue/perseverance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid buying or trusting impostor prayers and religious articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not buy prayers or religious articles from unknown sellers or be taken in by impostors who promise miraculous protections or guarantees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring suspicious prayers/articles to a priest for opinion; give alms to recognized charitable institutions or parish poor-box rather than to door-to-door peddlers; beware of persons selling 'miraculous' prayers or items for profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended standard prayers
rubrics_metrics.description: The prayers most recommended are the Lord's Prayer, the Hail Mary, the Apostles' Creed, the Confiteor, and the Acts of Faith, Hope, Love, and Contrition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are particularly commended as foundational prayers to form devotion and doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayers with willful distractions are invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: Prayers said with willful distractions—knowingly thinking of something else while praying—are of no avail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot pray with reverence and attention, postpone the prayer; God does not require fixed times but demands reverence when praying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rosary structure and use
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rosary comprises mysteries to be meditated upon: Joyful, Sorrowful, and Glorious mysteries (five of each set listed); generally the beads represent one third of the Rosary (five mysteries), so saying the beads three times covers the whole Rosary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order/days: Monday—Joyful, Tuesday—Sorrowful, Wednesday—Glorious; Thursday—Joyful, Friday—Sorrowful, Saturday—Glorious. On Sundays (except Advent/Lent) say Glorious; Advent: Joyful daily; Lent: Sorrowful daily; Eastertime: Glorious daily. When saying the Rosary, stop after mentioning each Mystery and meditate on its lesson before reciting the Our Father and Hail Marys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of common sacred monograms (I.N.R.I., I.H.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: I.N.R.I. appears on the Cross (Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews). I.H.S. with a cross is an abbreviation of Jesus (original Greek) and may also be read as first letters of Latin 'Jesus, Savior of men'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cross over I.H.S. can signify salvation by Christ's death; these inscriptions are suitable on altars and holy things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scapulars: meaning, wearing, and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The scapular is a sacramental worn to indicate placing oneself under the special protection of the Blessed Virgin; the small scapular is two small pieces of cloth joined over the shoulders and worn under ordinary garments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brown scapular = Scapular of Mount Carmel (devotion to Blessed Virgin); Church grants privileges and indulgences for wearing scapulars. Scapular is a 'uniform' of special devotion; multiple colored scapulars (red, white, blue, black) honor different devotions; wearing several joined at the top are called the five scapulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven Dolors and dolor bead devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The seven dolors are chief sorrows of the Blessed Virgin (circumcision; flight into Egypt; losing Jesus in Jerusalem; seeing Christ carry the Cross; His death; taking Him down from the Cross; His burial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are special seven-dolor beads with seven medals depicting these sorrows and seven beads between medals; meditate at each medal on the corresponding sorrow and pray Hail Marys on intervening beads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacramentals vs charms: proper use and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Sacramentals (blessed medals, crosses, scapulars) are worn in honor of God, the Blessed Virgin, or saints and point to prayer; charms and superstitious objects worn for effect (expecting power in the object itself) are sinful when one expects help from the thing itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on sacramentals as magical protection—do not willfully expose oneself to danger because of them (e.g., swim if you cannot swim). Use natural means (doctors) when appropriate; do not purchase 'blessed' items from dubious sellers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of private revelations, dreams, and visions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary dreams are products of imagination; biblical dreams were often visions used by God, but God no longer commonly uses dreams to communicate; private revelations by holy people are not obligatory to believe unless the Church confirms them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about alleged revelations; accept what the Church teaches; do not adopt doubtful private revelations as required doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Commandment: forbids strange gods/idolatry
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Commandment: 'I am the Lord thy God: thou shalt not have strange gods before Me.' It forbids giving to a creature the honor due to God alone, false worship, or attributing to a creature a perfection belonging only to God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern examples: making dress, money, honor, society, or pleasure into one's 'god'; worship performed not as directed by the Church (false worship) is condemned. Fortune-tellers and similar practices attribute God's prerogatives to creatures and thus violate the Commandment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sins against the First Commandment (spells, charms, occult practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of spells and charms, belief in dreams as revelatory, consulting mediums, spiritists, fortune-tellers, etc., constitute sins against the First Commandment because they attribute to creatures perfections that belong to God alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such practices are deceptive and often fraudulent; the devil may aid some impostors. If God wished these means known, He would give the power to the Church. Avoid and do not pay for fortune-telling or spiritist services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sins against faith, hope, and charity as breaches of the First Commandment
rubrics_metrics.description: Sins against faith, hope, and charity are also sins against the First Commandment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A detailed treatment of how one may sin against faith: (1) by not trying to know what God has taught (neglecting instruction), (2) by refusing to believe what God has taught (abandoning the faith), (3) by neglecting to profess belief (failing to practice and witness the faith). Examples: idling in religious instruction, leaving the true religion, knowing obligations but not practicing them (e.g., neglect of Mass or sacraments).

rubrics_metrics.name: The two great commandments as summary of the law
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole law of God is contained in two Commandments: love the Lord thy God with whole heart, soul, strength, and mind; and love thy neighbor as thyself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All other commandments either help keep these two or show how to avoid what opposes them. The first three of the Ten Commandments refer to God (love), the last seven to neighbor (love).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Ten Commandments listed as moral law
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ten Commandments are enumerated (1. No strange gods; 2. Do not take God's name in vain; 3. Keep the Sabbath holy; 4. Honor father and mother; 5. Do not kill; 6. Do not commit adultery; 7. Do not steal; 8. Do not bear false witness; 9. Do not covet neighbor's wife; 10. Do not covet neighbor's goods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are the moral law given by God and confirmed by Christ; Church commandments are also binding and, when broken, may be mortal sins just as the Commandments of God.
